title: Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins (2016)
shortTitle: Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins — standing note
summary: A plaintiff suing over a statutory violation must show a concrete injury, not just a particularized one, and a bare procedural violation divorced from real harm does not satisfy Article III.
notes:
Key line: "Article III standing requires a concrete injury even in the context of a statutory violation." Justice Alito, for the Court.

Citation: 578 U.S. 330 (2016).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was Spokeo, Inc., which operates a people search engine that gathers information from many databases and sells profiles containing a person's address, phone number, marital status, age, occupation, finances and other details. Respondent was Thomas Robins, whose Spokeo profile contained false information. Robins alleged that Spokeo was a consumer reporting agency under the Fair Credit Reporting Act and had willfully failed to follow reasonable procedures to assure accuracy. He sued on his own behalf and for a class of similarly situated people, seeking statutory damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation.
sections.Material Facts: The Fair Credit Reporting Act of 1970 requires consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of consumer reports and creates a private right of action for willful violations, with statutory damages, costs, attorney's fees and possible punitive damages. Someone searched Spokeo for information about Robins, and the resulting profile stated that he was married, had children, was in his 50s, was employed, was relatively affluent and held a graduate degree. Robins alleged that all of this was false and that the inaccuracies harmed his employment prospects while he was unemployed. He alleged that Spokeo markets its services to employers evaluating prospective employees and others.
sections.Procedural History: Robins filed a class action in the Central District of California. The District Court dismissed for lack of standing, finding that he had not alleged an injury in fact. The Ninth Circuit reversed in 2014, reasoning that Robins alleged a violation of his own statutory rights and that his interest in the handling of his credit information was individualized rather than collective. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on November 2, 2015, and on May 16, 2016 vacated the judgment and remanded.
sections.Issue: The Fair Credit Reporting Act gives consumers a right to sue consumer reporting agencies that willfully fail to follow reasonable procedures to assure accuracy, and it provides statutory damages without proof of actual loss. The Ninth Circuit found standing because Robins alleged a violation of his own statutory rights and an individualized interest in his credit information. Does a plaintiff who alleges a willful violation of the Act's procedural requirements, and who has a statutory right to sue, satisfy Article III's injury-in-fact requirement without showing a concrete harm, or must the injury be both particularized and concrete?
sections.Holding: Not necessarily. Injury in fact requires an injury that is both concrete and particularized. The Ninth Circuit addressed only particularization. Congress may identify and elevate intangible harms, but Article III requires a concrete injury even in the context of a statutory violation, so a bare procedural violation without concrete harm does not suffice. The Ninth Circuit's judgment was vacated and the case remanded to decide whether Robins alleged a concrete injury.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Alito restated the three elements of standing and focused on injury in fact. Particularization means the injury affects the plaintiff in a personal and individual way; concreteness means the injury is real and not abstract. The Ninth Circuit conflated the two by treating Robins's individualized statutory right as enough. Concrete does not mean tangible. Intangible harms can be concrete, and in deciding whether they are, courts consider both history, asking whether the harm has a close relationship to harms traditionally recognized as a basis for suit, and the judgment of Congress, which is well positioned to identify harms that meet Article III's minimum. Congress may not, however, grant standing to a plaintiff who would not otherwise have it. A plaintiff cannot allege a bare procedural violation divorced from any concrete harm. Not every inaccuracy in a report causes harm; an incorrect zip code, for example, would be difficult to treat as a concrete injury. At the same time, a risk of real harm can sometimes satisfy concreteness, as with libel and slander per se, and Congress plainly sought to curb the dissemination of false information through the Act's procedures. The Court left it to the Ninth Circuit to apply these principles to Robins's allegations.

topics.lrs-n-standing-procedure: Procedural authorization alone does not remove the injury requirement.
topics.lrs-n-standing-injury: The note directs attention to concrete injury even for intangible harms.
topics.lrs-n-standing-congress: Spokeo holds that Congress cannot confer Article III standing by creating a statutory right and cause of action alone; the plaintiff still needs concrete harm.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 2. Justice Thomas concurred, distinguishing suits to vindicate private rights, where the violation itself is an injury, from suits to enforce public rights, where the plaintiff must show individual harm. Justice Ginsburg dissented, joined by Justice Sotomayor, agreeing with the majority's description of the concreteness requirement but concluding that Robins had alleged a concrete injury because misinformation about his education, family and income could damage his job search, so no remand was needed.
